cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Rou Gui Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken firmly overnight to a medium oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted medium; the roast is pushed a little further than for the floral strains to bring out the spice.
harvest_season: Spring, late April into May; a mid-to-late strain picked once, with the spring harvest the only one of note.
appearance_dry: Long, tightly rolled dark brown strips with a warm, sweet-spicy smell.
appearance_wet: Long, thick olive-brown leaves with strong red edges.
taste_profile: A warm cassia-cinnamon aroma with dried fruit and honey, a medium-full body with a faint peppery warmth, a toasty sweetness and a long, cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. The spice shows best from the third steep and in the cooled cup; a zisha pot kept for roasted oolong also suits this strain.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually released in autumn after a medium roast and a rest of a few months; the spice integrates with time, and lots from the previous year are common and often better. Keeps three to four years sealed and dry.
description:
Rou Gui Xiang, cinnamon fragrance, is the Phoenix dancong that drinkers of Wuyi tea recognise at once: a cassia-like warmth over honey and dried fruit, in the long-leaf Chaozhou style rather than the roasted Wuyi one. It shares a name with the Wuyi Rou Gui cultivar but is a different plant; the resemblance is in the aroma, which is why both got called cinnamon.

It is one of the ten classic Fenghuang aroma types and descends from a single selected tree of the Fenghuang Shui Xian population, propagated by cuttings and grown mainly in the mid and high gardens of the range. It is a strain that needs a bit of roast, so it is seldom made in the very light style that suits Ya Shi Xiang.

The leaf is withered, shaken firmly overnight to a medium oxidation, rolled into strips and given a medium charcoal roast, often in two passes, which turns the strain's natural spiciness into something like cassia bark and dried longan. In the cup the aroma is warm spice, the body is medium-full with honey and dried fruit, there is a faint peppery warmth on the tongue, and the finish is long and cooling.

Brew it with the Chaozhou method, plenty of leaf, boiling water, instant pours, and give it time: the spice comes forward from the third steep, and the cooled cup shows it best. It takes a zisha pot well, unusual for dancong, and runs eight infusions.

It is sold by year, mostly from autumn, and it rests well, so last year's tea is a fair buy and often a better one. It is a mid-priced strain and a good bridge for people coming to dancong from yancha. The obvious tasting is to put it next to a Wuyi Rou Gui and notice how the same word describes two very different teas; the other is Jiang Hua Xiang, the dancong family's other spicy aroma.
sources_note: Listed among the ten classic aroma types; the mother-tree site is not stated because sources differ.
